More generally, the peace which the Gospel proclaims both to Israel "that is near," and to the Gentiles who are "far off" (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Ac 2:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>). <div eID="gen16305" type="x-p"/>
entries.291fa63b96ba0233f74a6a1b0964ba7c7b3b2d6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9411"/><div sID="gen16306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9411"/><hi type="bold">20. when it cannot rest--</hi>rather, "for it can have no rest" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.20">Job 15:20</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Pr 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.17">17</reference>). English Version represents the sea as occasionally agitated; but the Hebrew expresses that it can never be at rest. <div eID="gen16306" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5b961dd22939cec0d3c3c28497a8e1133dcb5a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9412"/><div sID="gen16307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9412"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.22">Is 48:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.9.22">2Ki 9:22</reference>).<div eID="gen16307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my God--</hi>The prophet, having God as his God, speaks in the person of Israel, prophetically regarded as having now appropriated God and His "peace" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.1-Isa.11.3">Is 11:1-3</reference>), warning the impenitent that, while they continue so, they can have no peace. <chapter eID="Isa.57"/>

entries.8fbb4f326e9e5fb946b0b468843574e94b49745b: <div eID="gen28749" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28750" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28751" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28751" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28750" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28752" type="x-p"/> After mentioning the removal of righteous persons as an awful symptom of the approach of Divine judgments, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa 57:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa 57:2</reference>, the prophet goes on to charge the nation in general with idolatry, and with courting the unprofitable alliance of idolatrous kings, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.3-Isa.57.12">Isa 57:3-12</reference>. In opposition to such vain confidence, the prophet enjoins trust in God, with whom the penitent and humble are sure to find acceptance, and from whom they should obtain temporal and spiritual deliverances, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.13-Isa.57.19">Isa 57:13-19</reference>. Awful condition of the wicked and finally impenitent, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.20">Isa 57:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.21">Isa 57:21</reference>. <div eID="gen28752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28753" type="x-p"/> I shall give Bishop Lowth's translation of the two first verses, and give the substance of his criticisms with additional evidence. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Isa 57:1</reference>. The righteous man perisheth, and no one considereth;And pious men are taken away, and no one understandeth,That the righteous man is taken away because of the evil. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa 57:2</reference>. He shall go in peace: he shall rest in his bed;Even the perfect man: he that walketh in the straight path. <div eID="gen28753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28754" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen28754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28755" type="x-p"/> The righteous perisheth - הצדק אבד hatstsadik abad. There is an emphasis here which seems intended to point out a particular person. See below. Perisheth - As the root אבד abad signifies the straying of cattle, their passing away from one pasture to another, I feel inclined to follow the grammatical meaning of the word "perish," pereo. So the Vulgate, justus periit, from per, By or Through, and eo, to Go. In his death the righteous man may be said to have passed through life, and to have passed by men, i.e., gone or passed before them into the eternal world. A similar mode of speech is used by our Saxon ancestors to express death: he went out of sight; and he went away; and to fare forth, to die. <div eID="gen28755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28756" type="x-p"/> There are very few places in Isaiah where Jesus Christ is not intended; and I am inclined to think that He is intended here, That Just One; and perhaps Stephen had this place in view, when he thus charged the Jews, "Ye denied τον ἁγιον και δικαιον, that Holy and Just One," <reference osisRef="Act.3.14">Act 3:14</reference>. That his death was not laid to heart by the wicked Jewish people, needs no proof. <div eID="gen28756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28757" type="x-p"/> Merciful men - If the first refers to Christ, this may well refer to the apostles. and to others of the primitive Christians, who were taken away, some by death and martyrdom, and others by a providential escape from the city that they knew was devoted to destruction. <div eID="gen28757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28758" type="x-p"/> The evil to come - That destruction which was to come upon this disobedient people by the Romans.
entries.aeeedbb7815178d95877c459bc532aa967081388: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28759" type="x-p"/> He shalt enter into peace "He shall go in peace" - יבוא שלום yabo shalom; the expression is elliptical, such as the prophet frequently uses. The same sense is expressed at large and in full terms, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.15">Gen 15:15</reference> : ואתה תבא אל אבותיך בשלום veattah libbo al abotheycha beshalom, "and thou shalt go to thy fathers in peace." <div eID="gen28759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28760" type="x-p"/> They shall rest in their beds, each one walking in his uprightness "He shall rest in his bed; even the perfect man" - This obscure sentence is reduced to a perfectly good sense, and easy construction by an ingenious remark of Dr. Durell. He reads ינוח על משכבו תם yanuach al mishcabo tam, "the perfect man shall rest in his bed." Two MSS. (one of them ancient) have ינוח yanuach, singular; and so the Vulgate renders it, requiescat, "he shall rest." The verb was probably altered to make it plural, and so consistent with what follows after the mistake had been made in the following words, by uniting משכבו mishcabo and תם tam into one word. See Merrick's Annotations on the Psalms, Addenda; where the reader will find that J. S. Moerlius, by the same sort of correction, and by rescuing the adjective תם tam, which had been swallowed up in another word in the same manner, has restored to a clear sense a passage before absolutely unintelligible: - למו חרצבות אין כי lemo chartsubboth ein ki :אולם ובריא תם ulam ubari tham "For no distresses happen to them; <div eID="gen28760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28761" type="x-p"/> Perfect and firm is their strength." <reference osisRef="Psa.73.4">Psa 73:4</reference>. <div eID="gen28761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28762" type="x-p"/> To follow on my application of this to our Lord: - He, the Just One, shall enter into peace - the peaceable, prosperous possession of the glorious mediatorial kingdom. They shall rest upon their beds - the hand of wrong and oppression can reach these persecuted followers of Christ no more. (But see below.) The perfect man walking in his uprightness. This may be considered as a general declaration. The separated spirit, though disunited from its body walking in conscious existence in the paradise of God, reaping the fruit of righteousness. The word which we render their beds, משכבותם mishkebotham, the learned bishop supposes to be two words; and to be compounded of משכבו mishkabo, his bed, and תם tam, the upright or perfect man. This is the reading both of the Syriac and Vulgate, and it is favored by the Chaldee: and one of De Rossi's MS. has משכבו mishkabo, his bed, without the word תם tam, which has been added by a later hand. Bishop Lowth, as we have seen, adopts this separation of the word and for ינוחו yanuchu, they shall rest, reads ינוה yanuach, he shall rest, which is supported by two of Dr. Kennicott's MSS., and by the Vulgate, Septuagint, and Arabic. The word תם tam, taken from משכבותם mishkebotham, should begin the latter clause of the verse; and then the interpolated words, each one, which our translators supplied, may be very well spared. The verse may be then read and paraphrased thus; - <div eID="gen28762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28763" type="x-p"/> He shall enter into peace: he shall rest upon his bed; <div eID="gen28763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28764" type="x-p"/> The perfect man walking in his uprightness. <div eID="gen28764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28765" type="x-p"/> The bed must signify the grave; the walking in uprightness after death, the conscious existence of the happy spirit, and its eternal progression in happiness and perfection: נכחו nechocho, straight before him; proceeding into the unlimited extent of eternal glory, increasing in happiness, and increasing in perfection. <div eID="gen28765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28766" type="x-p"/> My old MS. Bible translates very nervously: - <div eID="gen28766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28767" type="x-p"/> The rigtwise man perishith, <div eID="gen28767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28768" type="x-p"/> And there is not that bethinke in his herte. <div eID="gen28768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28769" type="x-p"/> And men of mercy ben gedrid, <div eID="gen28769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28770" type="x-p"/> For there is not that understonde: <div eID="gen28770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28771" type="x-p"/> From the face of malice, <div eID="gen28771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28772" type="x-p"/> Gedreid is the rigtwise. <div eID="gen28772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28773" type="x-p"/> Cumm pese: reste it in his bed <div eID="gen28773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28774" type="x-p"/> That geede in his rigt rewlinge. <div eID="gen28774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28775" type="x-p"/> It has been often remarked that, previously to the execution of God's judgments upon a wicked place, he has removed good men from it, that they might not suffer with the wicked. When great and good men are removed by death, or otherwise, from any place, the remaining inhabitants have much cause to tremble.
entries.a00906e6a3babeaa121721bc1a6d31bd219ee004: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28776" type="x-p"/> Among the smooth stones of the stream "Among the smooth stones of the valley" - The Jews were extremely addicted to the practice of many superstitious and idolatrous rites, which the prophet here inveighs against with great vehemence. Of the worship of rude stones consecrated, there are many testimonials of the ancients. They were called βαιτυλοι and βαιτυλια· probably from the stone which Jacob erected at Beth-el, pouring oil upon the top of it. This practice was very common in different ages and places. Arnobius, lib. i., gives an account of his own practice in this respect before he became a Christian: Si quando conspexeram lubricatum lapidem, et ex olivi unguine sordidatum; tanquam inesset vis praesens, adulabar, affabar, et beneficia poscebam nihil sentiente de trunco. "When I have met with a smooth stone, smeared with oil, supposing a spiritual power to be connected with it, I worshipped it, paid my addresses to it, and requested blessings," etc. Clemens Alex., Strom. lib. vii., speaks of a worshipper of every smooth stone in a proverbial way, to denote one given up to superstition. And accordingly Theophrastus has marked this as one strong feature in the character of the superstitious man: Και των λιπαρων λιθων των εν ταις τριοδοις παριων, εκ της ληκυθου ελαιου καταχειν, και επι γονατα πεσων και προσκυνησας απαλλαττεσθαι. "Passing by the anointed stones in the streets, he takes out his phial of oil, and pours it on them; and having fallen on his knees, and made his adorations, he departs. "Kimchi says: "When they found a beautiful polished stone in a brook or river, they paid Divine adoration to it." This idolatry is still prevalent among the Hindoos. The stone which is the object of their adoration is called salgram. They are found about eighty miles from the source of the river Sown, in the viceroyalty of Bahar, on the coast of Bengal. Ayeen Akbery vol. 2 p. 29.
entries.bdfcb240ac13a53ab83a451bfa538dd9e833c90b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen28776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28777" type="x-p"/> Behind the doors also and the posts hast thou set up thy remembrance "Behind the door, and the door-posts, hast thou set up thy memorial" - That is, the image of their tutelary gods, or something dedicated to them; in direct opposition to the law of God, which commanded them to write upon the door-posts of their house, and upon their gates, the words of God's law; <reference osisRef="Deu.6.9">Deu 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.11.20">Deu 11:20</reference>. If they chose for them such a situation as more private, it was in defiance of a particular curse denounced in the law against the man who should make a graven or a molten image, and put it in a secret place; <reference osisRef="Deu.27.15">Deu 27:15</reference>. An ancient MS., with another, has אחר achar, without the conjunction ו vau, and.
entries.47252e205440afe07fcb4daef6254b13c588cdb5: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28778" type="x-p"/> And thou wentest to the king with ointment "And thou hast visited the king with a present of oil" - That is, the king of Assyria, or Egypt. Hosea, chap, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Hos 12:1</reference>, reproaches the Israelites for the same practice: - "They make a covenant with Assyria, <div eID="gen28778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28779" type="x-p"/> And oil is carried to Egypt." <div eID="gen28779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28780" type="x-p"/> It is well known, that in all parts of the east, whoever visits a great person must carry him a present. "It is counted uncivil," says Maundreg, p. 26, "to visit in this country without an offering in hand. All great men expect it as a tribute due to their character and authority; and look upon themselves as affronted, and indeed defrauded, when the compliment is omitted." Hence שור shur, to visit a person, is equivalent to making him a present; and תשורה teshurah signifies a present made on such occasions; as our translators have rightly rendered it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.7">1Sam 9:7</reference>; on which Jarchi says Menachem exponit תשורה teshurah, quod significat oblationem sive manus, ut aliquis aspiciat faciem regis, aut alicuius magnatis. "Menachem expounds תשורה teshurah of an offering or gift which is presented in order to be admitted into the presence of the king or some great man."
entries.6863919a6b980a2a80b419a69a52de75b23c679e: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen28780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28781" type="x-p"/> Yet saidst thou not, There is no hope "Thou hast said, There is hope" - In one of the MSS. at Koningsberg, collated by Lilienthal, the words לא אמרת lo amarta, are left in the text unpointed, as suspected; and in the margin the corrector has written ותאמרי vattomari. Now if we compare <reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jer 2:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.18.12">Jer 18:12</reference>, we shall find that the subject is in both places quite the same with this of Isaiah; and the sentiment expressed, that of a desperate resolution to continue at all hazards in their idolatrous practices; the very thing that in all reason we might expect here. Probably, therefore, the latter is the true reading in this place. - L.
entries.5dc5d81370104483bd59178639c767fd02398adc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28782" type="x-p"/> For laid it to thy heart "Nor revolved it in thy hand" - Eight MSS., (four ancient), and the two oldest editions, with another, add the conjunction ו vau, ולא velo: which is confirmed by all the ancient Versions. <div eID="gen28782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28783" type="x-p"/> Even of old "And winked" - For ומעולם umeolam, which makes no good sense or construction in this place, twenty-three MSS. (seven ancient) and three editions have מעלם, (to be thus pointed מעלם malim); Παρορω, Septuagint; quasi non videns, "as if not seeing," Vulgate. See <reference osisRef="Psa.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>. The truth of this reading, so confirmed, admits of no doubt. In one of my own MSS. the ו vau has been written, but afterwards struck out. Is it not because I was silent, and winked?
entries.e103b22a3d11b66de67e7fa559fb961be4ad1283: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28784" type="x-p"/> Thy righteousness "My righteousness" - For צדקתך tsidkathech, Thy righteousness, the Syriac, Septuagint, MSS. Alex. and Pachom., and 1. D. II., and Marchal. and οἱ Γ, and the Arabics read צדקי tsidki, My righteousness.
entries.2c069eb6f70d5d79bb984df067cc573bbe8eff65: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen28784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28785" type="x-p"/> Let thy companies deliver thee "Let thine associates deliver thee" - Thirty-nine MSS. (ten ancient) of Dr. Kennicott's, and two of my own, and the two oldest editions have יצילכו yatstsiluchu, plural.
entries.0614e569654966ab315bf1cf398932d95db91cd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen28785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28786" type="x-p"/> And shall say "Then will I say" - ואמר vaomer, to be pointed as the first person future. They are the words of God, as it is plain from the conclusion of the verse; my people, עמי ammi.
entries.432d4b96dc52cc7e983530f467c6f88bd441f592: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen28786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28787" type="x-p"/> For thus saith the high and lofty One "For thus saith Jehovah, the high and the lofty" - A MS. adds יהוה Yehovah, after אמר amar, and edition Prag. 1518. So the Septuagint, Alex., and Arabic. An ancient MS. adds יה Yah. <div eID="gen28787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28788" type="x-p"/> With him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit - Twelve MSS. have את eth, without the conjunction ו vau. Pro ואת veeth, forte legendum ואראה veerah: confer <reference osisRef="Psa.113.5">Psa 113:5</reference>, et <reference osisRef="Psa.138.6">Psa 138:6</reference>. - Secker. "We should perhaps read ואראה veerah, instead of ואת veeth. See <reference osisRef="Psa.113.5">Psa 113:5</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Psa.138.6">Psa 138:6</reference>."
entries.05c2c28ba0ff33cae8013acb899930c128f95f4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen28788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28789" type="x-p"/> For I will not contend for ever - The learned have taken a great deal of pains to little purpose on the latter part of this verses which they suppose to be very obscure. After all their labors upon it, I think the best and easiest explication of it is given in the two following elegant passages of the Psalms, which I presume are exactly parallel to it, and very clearly express the same sentiment. "But he in his tender mercy will forgive their sin <div eID="gen28789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28790" type="x-p"/> And will not destroy them; <div eID="gen28790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28791" type="x-p"/> Yea, oftentimes will he turn away his wrath, <div eID="gen28791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28792" type="x-p"/> And will not rouse up his indignation: <div eID="gen28792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28793" type="x-p"/> For he remembereth that they are but flesh, <div eID="gen28793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28794" type="x-p"/> A breath that passeth, and returneth not." <reference osisRef="Psa.78.38">Psa 78:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.78.39">Psa 78:39</reference>. "He will not always contend <div eID="gen28794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28795" type="x-p"/> Neither will he for ever hold his wrath: <div eID="gen28795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28796" type="x-p"/> As a father yearneth towards his children, <div eID="gen28796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28797" type="x-p"/> So is Jehovah tenderly compassionate towards them that fear him For he knoweth our frame; <div eID="gen28797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28798" type="x-p"/> He remembereth that we are but dust." <reference osisRef="Psa.103.9">Psa 103:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.13">Psa 103:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference>. <div eID="gen28798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28799" type="x-p"/> In the former of these two passages the second line seems to be defective both in measure and sense. I suppose the word אותם otham, then is lost at the end; which seems to be acknowledged by the Chaldee and Vulgate, who render as if they had read ולא ישחית אותם velo yaschith otham. - L. <div eID="gen28799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28800" type="x-p"/> For the spirit - רוח ruach, the animal life. <div eID="gen28800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28801" type="x-p"/> And the souls - נשמות neshamoth, the immortal spirits. The Targum understands this of the resurrection. I will restore the souls of the dead, i.e., to their bodies.
entries.5840aa9f7d009585820d2279e3ff4a7982ecb058: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen28801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28802" type="x-p"/> For the iniquity of his covetousness was I wroth "Because of his iniquity for a short time was I wroth" - For בצעו bitso, I read בצע betsa, a little while, from בצע batsa, he cut of, as the Septuagint read and render it, βραχυ τι, "a certain short space." Propter iniquitatem avaritiae ejus, "because of the iniquity of his avarice," the rendering of the Vulgate, which our translators and I believe all others follow, is surely quite beside the purpose.
entries.1f469b3e8d4b0788d52e3449bea33cd4ce4ac99c: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen28802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28803" type="x-p"/> I have seen his ways - Probably these verses refer to the restoration of the Jews from captivity.
entries.2f56501826d388b2a86d5f416b0789eca5a33655: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen28803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28804" type="x-p"/> I create the fruit of the lips - "The sacrifice of praise," saith St. Paul, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb 13:15</reference>, "is the fruit of the lips." God creates this fruit of the lips, by giving new subject and cause of thanksgiving by his mercies conferred on those among his people, who acknowledge and bewail their transgressions, and return to him. The great subject of thanksgiving is peace, reconciliation and pardon, offered to them that are nigh, and to them that are afar off, not only to the Jew, but also to the Gentile, as St. Paul more than once applies those terms, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.13">Eph 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Eph 2:17</reference>. See also <reference osisRef="Act.2.39">Act 2:39</reference>. <div eID="gen28804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28805" type="x-p"/> Peace to him that is far off "That is, to the penitent; and to him that is near, i.e., the righteous." - Kimchi.
entries.98fb448e5d3a406ee77d976fcf1432540c1496a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen28805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28806" type="x-p"/> There is no peace, saith my God - For אלהי Elohai, twenty-two MSS. (five ancient) of Kennicott's, thirty of De Rossi's, and one ancient of my own, read יהוה Yehovah; the Vulgate, Septuagint, Alex., and Arabic, and three MSS. have both. This verse has reference to the nineteenth. The perseveringly wicked and impenitent are excluded from all share in that peace above mentioned, that reconcilement and pardon which is promised to the penitent only. The forty-eighth chapter ends with the same declaration, to express the exclusion of the unbelievers and impenitent from the benefit of the foregoing promises. - L.  <chapter eID="Isa.57"/> <div eID="gen28806" type="x-p"/>

entries.e14b0753621a984e1245507504fcd06eb15e9c73: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1-Isa.57.2">Isa 57:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13561" type="x-p"/> Whilst watchmen and shepherds, prophets and rulers, without troubling themselves about the flock which they have to watch and feed, are thus indulging their own selfish desires, and living in debauchery, the righteous man is saved by early death from the judgment, which cannot fail to come with such corruption as this. <hi type="italic">“The righteous perisheth, and no man taketh it to heart; and pious men are swept away, without any one considering that the righteous is swept away from misfortune. He entereth into peace: they rest upon their beds, whoever has walked straight before him.”</hi> With “the righteous” the prophet introduces, in glaring contrast to this luxurious living on the part of the leading men of the nation, the standing figure used to denote the fate of its best men. With this prevailing demoralization and worldliness, the righteous succumbs to the violence of both external and internal sufferings. אבד, he dies before his time (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ecc 7:15</reference>); from the midst of the men of his generation he is carried away from this world (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>; Mic 7:2), and no one lays it to heart, viz., the divine accusation and threat involved in this early death. Men of piety (<hi type="italic">chesed</hi>, the love of God and man) are swept away, without there being any one to understand or consider that (<hi type="italic">kı̄</hi> unfolds the object to be considered and laid to heart, viz., what is involved in this carrying away when regarded as a providential event) the righteous is swept away “from the evil,” i.e., that he may be saved from the approaching punishment (compare 2Ki 22:20). For the prevailing corruption calls for punishment from God; and what is first of all to be expected is severe judgment, through which the coming salvation will force its way. In <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa 57:2</reference> it is intimated that the righteous man and the pious do not lose the blessings of this salvation because they lose this life: for whereas, according to the prophet’s watchword, there is no peace to the wicked, it is true, on the other hand, of the departing righteous man, that “he enters into peace” (<hi type="italic">shâlōm</hi>, <hi type="italic">acc. loci s. status</hi>; Ges. 118, 1); “they rest upon their beds,” viz., the bottom of the grave, which has become their <hi type="italic">mishkâb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.17.13">Job 17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.26">Job 21:26</reference>), “however has walked in that which lay straight before him,” i.e., the one straight plain path which he had set before him (נכחו <hi type="italic">acc. obj.</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Isa 50:10</reference>, Ewald, §172, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, from נכח, that which lies straight before a person; whereas נכח with נכח נכחו, signifying probably fixedness, steadiness of look, related to Arab. <hi type="italic">nkḥ</hi>, to pierce, נכה, <hi type="italic">percutere</hi>, is used as a preposition: compare <reference osisRef="Prov.4.25">Pro 4:25</reference>, לנכח, straight or exactly before him). The grave, when compared with the restlessness of this life, is therefore “peace.” He who has died in faith rests in God, to whom he has committed himself and entrusted his future. We have here the glimmering light of the New Testament consolation, that the death of the righteous is better than life in this world, because it is the entrance into peace.
entries.19e3846b63c0e640d51c4ada322058e71de6b97f: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.3-Isa.57.4">Isa 57:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen13561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13562" type="x-p"/> The reproachful language of the prophet is now directed against the mass of the nation, who have occasioned the “evil” from which the righteous is swept away, i.e., the generation that is hostile to the servants of Jehovah, and by whom those sins of idolatry are still so shamelessly carried on, which first led to the captivity. <hi type="italic">“And ye, draw nearer hither, children of the sorceress, seed of the adulterer, and of her that committed whoredom! Over whom do ye make yourselves merry? Over whom do ye open the mouth wide, and put the tongue out long? Are ye not the brook of apostasy, seed of lying?”</hi> They are to draw nearer hither (<hi type="italic">hēnnâh</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Gen.15.16">Gen 15:16</reference>), to the place where God is speaking through His prophet, to have themselves painted, and to hear their sentence. Just as elsewhere the moral character of a man is frequently indicated by the mention of his father (2Ki 6:32), or his mother (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.30">1Sa 20:30</reference>), or both parents (<reference osisRef="Job.30.8">Job 30:8</reference>), so here the generation of the captivity, so far as it continued to practise the idolatry by which its ancestors had brought upon themselves the Chaldean catastrophe, is called <hi type="italic">first</hi> עננה בּני (or more correctly עננה), sons of the sorceress (possibly the maker of clouds or storm, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference>, Jer. <hi type="italic">auguratricis</hi>), one who made heathen and superstitious customs her means of livelihood, viz., the community as it existed before the captivity, which really deserved no better name, on account of the crying contradiction between its calling and its conduct; and <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, with regard to both the male and female members of the community, ותּזנה מנאף זרע, <hi type="italic">semen adulteri et fornicariae</hi> (Jer.), though Stier, Hahn, and others adopt the rendering <hi type="italic">semen adulterum et quod </hi>(<hi type="italic">qui</hi>)<hi type="italic">scortaris</hi>. A better rendering than this would be, “Seed of an adulterer, and one who committest adultery thyself,” viz., (what would be indicated with this explanation by the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi>) in consequence of this descent from an adulterer. But as זרע (seed, posterity), wherever it is more minutely defined, is connected with a genitive, and not with an adjective, the presumption is that ותזנה מנאף denotes the father and mother. ותּזנה is an attributive clause regarded as a genitive (Ges. §123, 3, Anm. 1), and more closely connected with מנאף htiw than if it was written ותזנה = וזונה, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.21">Isa 1:21</reference>): Seed of an adulterer, and consequently (Ewald, §351,<hi type="italic">b</hi>), or similarly, of one who gave herself up to whoredom. Idolatry, prostitution, and magic are most closely allied. The prophet now asks, “Over whom do ye find your pleasure? For whom are your common contemptuous actions intended?” התענּג is only used here, and denotes the feeling which finds pleasure in the sufferings of another. The objects of this malicious contemptuous pleasure (Psa 22:8., <reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>) are the servants of Jehovah; and the question, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.23">Isa 37:23</reference>, is one of amazement at their impudence, since the men over whom they make merry are really deserving of esteem, whereas they themselves are the refuse of Israel: Are ye not a brook of apostasy, seed of lying? As apostasy and lying, when regarded as parents, can only produce something resembling themselves; the character of those from whom they are descended is here imputed to the men themselves, even more clearly than before. The genitives of origin are also genitives of attribute. Instead of ילדי (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference>) we have here ילדי before <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi>, with the shortening of <hi type="italic">a</hi> into <hi type="italic">i</hi>.
entries.03c34641ea237ecce727036e5b6010794b409bac: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.5-Isa.57.6">Isa 57:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen13562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13563" type="x-p"/> The participles which follow in the next v. are in apposition to אתּ, and confirm the predicates already applied to them. They soon give place, however, to independent sentences. <hi type="italic">“Ye that inflame yourselves by the terebinths, under every green tree, ye slayers of children in the valleys under the clefts of the rocks. By the smooth ones of the brook was thy portion; they, they were thy lot: thou also pouredst out libations to them, thou laidst meat-offerings upon them. Shall I be contented with this?”</hi> The people of the captivity are addressed, and the idolatry handed down to them from their ancestors depicted. The prophet looks back from the standpoint of the captivity, and takes his colours from the time in which he himself lived, possibly from the commencement of Manasseh’s reign, when the heathenism that had for a long time been suppressed burst forth again in all its force, and the measure of iniquity became full. The <hi type="italic">part. niphal</hi> הנּחמים is formed like נחן in <reference osisRef="Jer.22.23">Jer 22:23</reference>, if the latter signifies <hi type="italic">miserandum esse</hi>. The primary form is נחם, which is doubled like נגּר from גּרר in <reference osisRef="Job.20.28">Job 20:28</reference>, and from which נחם is formed by the resolution of the latent reduplication. Stier derives it from; but even if formed from this, נחם would still have to be explained from נחם, after the form נצּת. <hi type="italic">'Elı̄m</hi> signifies either gods or terebinths. But although it might certainly mean idols, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Dan 11:36</reference> (lxx, Targ., and Jerome), it is never used directly in this sense, and Isaiah always uses the word as the name of a tree (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa 61:3</reference>). The terebinths are introduced here, exactly as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>, as an object of idolatrous lust: “who inflame themselves with the terebinths;” ב denotes the object with which the lust is excited and inf <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi>. The terebinth (<hi type="italic">'ēlâh</hi>) held the chief place in tree-worship (hence אלנם, lit., oak-trees, together with אלם, is the name of one of the Phoenician gods),<note placement="foot">See Levy, <hi type="italic">Phönizische Studien</hi>, i. 19.</note> possibly as being the tree sacred to Astarte; just as the <hi type="italic">Samura Acacia</hi> among the heathen Arabs was the tree sacred to the goddess <hi type="italic">'Uzza</hi>.<note placement="foot">Krehl, <hi type="italic">Religioin der vorisl</hi>. Araber, p. 74ff.</note> <div eID="gen13563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13564" type="x-p"/> The following expression, “under every green tree,” is simply a permutative of the words “with the terebinths” in the sense of “with the terebinths, yea, under every green tree” (a standing expression from <reference osisRef="Deut.12.2">Deu 12:2</reference> downwards) - one tree being regarded as the abode and favourite of this deity, and another of that, and all alluring you to your carnal worship. <div eID="gen13564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13565" type="x-p"/> From the tree-worship with its orgies, which was so widely spread in antiquity generally, the prophet passes to the leading Canaanitish abomination, viz., human sacrifices, which had been adopted by the Israelites (along with שׁחטי we find the false reading שׂחטי, which is interpreted as signifying self-abuse). Judging from the locality named, “under the clefts of the rocks,” the reference is not to the slaying of children sacrificed to Moloch in the valley of Hinnom, but to those offered to Baal upon his <hi type="italic">bâmōth</hi> or high places (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.5">Jer 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.20-Ezek.16.21">Eze 16:20-21</reference>; Hos 13:2; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.37-Ps.106.38">Psa 106:37-38</reference>). As we learn from the <hi type="italic">chronique scandaleuse</hi> many things connected with the religious history of Israel, which cannot be found in its historical books, there is nothing to surprise us in the stone-worship condemned in Isa 57:6. The <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> of חלּקי is in any case <hi type="italic">dagesh</hi> <hi type="italic">dirimens</hi>. The singular is wither חלק after the form חכמי (cf., עצבי, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa 58:3</reference>), or חלק after the form ילדי. But חלק, smoothness, never occurs; and the explanation, “in the smoothnesses, i.e., the smooth places of the valley, is thy portion,” has this also against it, that it does not do justice to the connection בּ חלק, in which the preposition is not used in a local sense, and that it leaves the emphatic הם הם quite unexplained. The latter does not point to places, but to objects of worship for which they had exchanged Jehovah, of whom the true Israelite could say ה חלקי, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.57">Psa 119:57</reference>, etc., or בה לי חלק, <reference osisRef="Josh.22.25">Jos 22:25</reference>, and גּורלי תּומיך אתּה (Thou art He that maintaineth my lot), Psa 16:5. The prophet had such expressions as these in his mind, and possibly also the primary meaning of גורל = κλῆρος, which may be gathered from the rare Arabic word <hi type="italic">'garal</hi>, gravel, stones worn smooth by rolling, when he said, “In the smooth ones of the valley is thy portion; they, they are thy lot.” In the Arabic also, <hi type="italic">achlaq</hi> (equilvaent to <hi type="italic">châlâq</hi>, smooth, which forms here a play upon the word with חלק, <hi type="italic">châlâq</hi>) is a favourite word for stones and rocks. חלּקי־נחל, however, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.40">1Sa 17:40</reference> (where the intensive form חלּוּק, like שׁכּוּל, is used), are stones which the stream in the valley has washed smooth with time, and rounded into a pleasing shape. The mode of the worship, the pouring out of libations,<note placement="foot">Compare the remarks made in the <hi type="italic">Comm. on the Pentateuch</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Gen.29.20">Gen 29:20</reference>, on the heathen worship of anointed stones, and the Baetulian worship.</note> and the laying of meat-offerings upon them, confirm this view. In Carthage such stones were called <hi type="italic">abbadires</hi> (= אדיר, אבן); and among the ancient Arabs, the <hi type="italic">asnâm</hi> or idols consisted for the most part of rude blocks of stone of this description. Herodotus (3:8) speaks of seven stones which the Arabs anointed, calling upon the god Orotal. Suidas (<hi type="italic">s.v.</hi> Θεῦς ἄρης) states that the idol of Ares in Petra was a black square stone; and the black stone of the <hi type="italic">Ka'aba</hi> was, according to a very inconvenient tradition for the Mohammedans, an idol of Saturn (<hi type="italic">zuhal</hi>).<note placement="foot">See Krehl, p. 72. In the East Indies also we find stone-worship not only among the Vindya tribes (Lassen, <hi type="italic">A.K.</hi> i. 376), but also among the Vaishnavas, who worship Vishnu in the form of a stone, viz., the <hi type="italic">sâlagrâm</hi>, a kind of stone from the river Gandak (see Wilson’s <hi type="italic">Sanscrit Lexicon s.h.v</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Vishnu</hi>-<hi type="italic">Purân</hi>, p. 163). The fact of the great antiquity of stone and tree worship has been used in the most ridiculous manner by Dozy in his work on the Israelites at Mecca (1864). He draws the following conclusion from <reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">Deu 32:18</reference> : “Thus the Israelites sprang from a divine block of stone; and this is, in reality, the true old version of the origin of the nation.” From <reference osisRef="Isa.51.1-Isa.51.2">Isa 51:1-2</reference>, he infers that Abraham and Sara were not historical persons at all, but that the former was a block of stone, and the latter a hollow; and that the two together were a block of stone in a hollow, to which divine worship was paid. “This fact,” he says, “viz. that Abraham and Sarah in the second Isaiah are not historical persons, but a block of stone and a hollow, is one of great worth, as enabling us to determine the time at which the stories of Abraham in Genesis were written, and to form a correct idea of the spirit of those stories.”</note> <div eID="gen13565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13566" type="x-p"/> Stone-worship of this kind had been practised by the Israelites before the captivity, and their heathenish practices had been transmitted to the exiles in Babylon. The meaning of the question, Shall I comfort myself concerning such things? - i.e., Shall I be contented with them (אנּחם <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, not <hi type="italic">hithpael</hi>)? - is, that it was impossible that descendants who so resembled their fathers should remain unpunished.
entries.ffa7250aff81d120565865afeb6ecd873b357be4: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.7-Isa.57.8">Isa 57:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13567" type="x-p"/> The prophet now proceeds with perfects, like שׁפכתּ and העלית (addressed to the national community generally, the congregation regarded as a woman). The description is mostly retrospective. <hi type="italic">“Upon a lofty and high mountain hast thou set up thy bed; thou also ascendedst thither to offer slain offerings. And behind the door and the post thou didst place thy reminder: for thou uncoveredst away from me, and ascendedst; thou madest thy bed broad, and didst stipulate for thyself what they had to do: thou lovedst their lying with thee; thou sawest their manhood.”</hi> The lovers that she sought for herself are the gods of the heathen. Upon lofty mountains, where they are generally worshipped, did she set up her bed, and did all that was needed to win their favour. The <hi type="italic">zikkârōn</hi>, i.e., the declaration that Jehovah is the only God, which the Israelites were to write upon the posts of their houses, and upon the entrances (<reference osisRef="Deut.6.9">Deu 6:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.20">Deu 11:20</reference>), for a constant reminder, she had put behind the door and post, that she might not be reminded, to her shame, of her unfaithfulness. That this explanation, which most of the commentators adopt, is the true one, is proved by the expression מאתּי כּי which follows, and according to which זכרון is something inconvenient, which might and was intended to remind them of Jehovah. מאתּי, away, far from me, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.1">Jer 3:1</reference>, and like מתּחתּי, which is still more frequently used. It is unnecessary to take <hi type="italic">gillı̄th</hi> with ערותך understood (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.18">Eze 23:18</reference>) as equivalent to “thou makest thyself naked,” or with reference to the clothes = ἀνασύρεις. משׁכּב is the common object of all three verbs, even of ותּעלי (with double <hi type="italic">metheg</hi>), after Gen 49:4. On ותּכרת for ותּכרתי (cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.3.5">Jer 3:5</reference>), see Ewald, §191, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The explanation “thou didst bind,” or “thou didst choose (some) of them to thyself,” is contrary to the general usage, according to which ל כּרת signifies <hi type="italic">spondere</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.7.18">2Ch 7:18</reference>), and (עם כּרת <hi type="italic">pacisci</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.8">1Sa 22:8</reference>), in both cases with בּרית to be supplied, so that מן (בּרית) כּרת would mean <hi type="italic">stipulari ab aliquo</hi>, i.e., to obtain from a person a solemn promise, with all the force of a covenant. What she stipulated from them was, either the wages of adultery, or the satisfaction of her wanton lust. What follows agrees with this; for it is there distinctly stated, that the lovers to whom she offered herself gratified her lust abundantly: <hi type="italic">adamasti concutibum eorum</hi> (<hi type="italic">mishkâb</hi>, cubile, e.g., <reference osisRef="Prov.7.17">Pro 7:17</reference>, and <hi type="italic">concubitus</hi>, e.g., Ezra 23:17), <hi type="italic">manum conspexisit</hi>. The Targum and Jewish commentators adopt this explanation, <hi type="italic">loco quem delegisti</hi>, or (<hi type="italic">postquam</hi>) <hi type="italic">locum delegisti</hi>. This also is apparently the meaning of the accents, and most of the more modern commentators have adopted it, taking יד in the sense of place or side. But this yields only a very lame and unmeaning thought. Doederlein conjectured that יד was employed here in the sense of ἰθύφαλλος; and this is the explanation adopted by Hitzig, Ewald, and others. The Arabic furnishes several analogies to this obscene use of the word; and by the side of <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.26">Eze 16:26</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.20">Eze 23:20</reference>, where the same thing is affirmed in even plainer language, there is nothing to astonish in the passage before us. The meaning is, that after the church of Jehovah had turned away from its God to the world and its pleasures, it took more and more delight in the pleasures afforded it by idolatry, and indulged its tastes to the full.
entries.264984e873edaa51a6d233a8af21922d8256b272: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.9-Isa.57.10">Isa 57:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen13567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13568" type="x-p"/> In the closest reciprocal connection with this God-forgetting, adulterous craving for the favour of heathen gods, stood their coquetting with the heathen power of the world. <hi type="italic">“And thou wentest to the king with oil, and didst measure copiously thy spices, and didst send thy messengers to a great distance, and didst deeply abase thyself, even to Hades. Thou didst become weary of the greatness of thy way; yet thou saidst not, It is unattainable: thou obtainedst the revival of thy strength: therefore thou wast not pained.”</hi> The first thing to be noticed here, is one that has been overlooked by nearly all the modern commentators, viz., that we have here a historical retrospect before us. And secondly, a single glance at <reference osisRef="Isa.57.11">Isa 57:11</reference> is sufficient to show that the words refer to a servile coquetry from the fear of man, and therefore to a wicked craving for the favour of man; so that “the king,” is not Baal, or any heathen god whatever (according to <reference osisRef="Isa.8.21">Isa 8:21</reference> and Zep 1:5), but the Asiatic ruler of the world. Ahaz sent messengers, as we read in 2Ki 16:7., to Tiglath-pileser, the king of Assyria, to say to Him, “I am thy servant and thy son.” And Ahaz took the silver and gold that were in the house of Jehovah, and in the treasures of the palace, and sent a bribe to the king of Assyria. And again, at 2Ki 16:10., Ahaz went to Damascus to meet the king of Assyria, and there he saw an altar, and sent a model of it to Jerusalem, and had one like it put in the place of the altar of burnt-offering. Such acts as these are here described in the figure of Israel travelling with oil to the king, and taking a quantity of choice spices with it to gain his favour, and also sending messengers, and not only bowing itself to the earth, but even stooping to Hades, that is to say, standing as it were on its head in its excessive servility, for the purpose of obtaining allies. It seems most natural to take בּשׁמן as equivalent to בשמן משׁוּחה: thou wentest in oil (dripping with pomade), and didst apply to thyself many spices; but <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> after verbs of going signifies to go with anything, to take it with one and bring it, so that the oil and spices are thought of here as presents, which she took with her as sensual stimulants, with a view to the amorous pleasures she was seeking (<reference osisRef="Ezek.23.41">Eze 23:41</reference>, cf., Hos 12:2). השׁפּיל signifies to go deep down in <reference osisRef="Jer.13.18">Jer 13:18</reference>; the meaning here is, to bow very low, or to degrade one’s self. By “the greatness or breadth of the way” (a similar expression to that in <reference osisRef="Josh.9.13">Jos 9:13</reference>), all the great sacrifices are intended which it cost her to purchase the favour of the heathen ruler. Although they were a great trouble to her, yet she did not say נואש, “it is hopeless;” the <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> of יאשׁ signifies in <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">1Sa 27:1</reference>, to betake one’s self to a thing with despair of its success. The participle in <reference osisRef="Job.6.26">Job 6:26</reference> means a despairing person; it also occurs in a neuter sense in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.26">Jer 2:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.12">Jer 18:12</reference>, viz., given up, i.e., absolutely in vain. She did not give up hope, although the offerings nearly exhausted her strength; on the contrary, she gained יד חיּת, “life of her arm,” i.e., (according to the use of חיה in the sense of reviving, and החיה, to bring to life again) new life in her arm, in other words, “the renewing of her strength” (<hi type="italic">recentem vigorem virium suarum</hi>). Thus, without noticing the sighs and groans forced from her by the excessive toil and fatigue, but stirring herself up again and again, she pursued the plan of strengthening her alliances with the heathen. Ezekiel’s picture of Aholah and Aholibah is like a commentary on <reference osisRef="Isa.57.3-Isa.57.10">Isa 57:3-10</reference> (see Ezek 23).
entries.72c70e1d172deb307b6264668dfe86ddef03e5cd: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.11">Isa 57:11</reference> <div eID="gen13568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13569" type="x-p"/> From fear of man, Israel, and still more Judah, had given up the fear of Jehovah. <hi type="italic">“And of whom hast thou been afraid, and </hi>(<hi type="italic">whom</hi>)<hi type="italic">didst thou fear, that thou becamest a liar, and didst not continue mindful of me, and didst not take it to heart?”</hi> It was of men - only mortal men, with no real power (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa 51:12</reference>) - that Israel was so needlessly afraid, that it resorted to lies and treachery to Jehovah (<hi type="italic">kı̄</hi>, <hi type="italic">ut</hi>, an interrogative sentence, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.18">2Sa 7:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>): purchasing the favour of man out of the fear of man, and throwing itself into the arms of false tutelar deities, it banished Jehovah its true shelter out of its memory, and did not take it to heart, viz., the sinfulness of such infidelity, and the eventful consequences by which it was punished (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7">Isa 47:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.42.25">Isa 42:25</reference>). <div eID="gen13569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13570" type="x-p"/> With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.11">Isa 57:11</reference></hi> the reproaches are addressed to the present. The treachery of Israel had been severely punished in the catastrophe of which the captivity was the result, but without effecting any improvement. The great mass of the people were as forgetful of God as ever, and would not be led to repentance by the long-suffering of God, which had hitherto spared them from other well-merited punishments. <hi type="italic">“Am I not silent, and that for a long time, whereas thou wast not afraid of me?”</hi> A comparison with <reference osisRef="Isa.42.14">Isa 42:14</reference> will show that the prophecy returns here to its ordinary style. The lxx and Jerome render the passage as if the reading were מעלם (viz., עיני = παρορῶν, <hi type="italic">quasi non videns</hi>), and this is the reading which Lowth adopts. We may see from this, that the original text had a defective ומעלם, which was intended, however, to be read וּמעלם. The prophet applies the term <hi type="italic">‛ōlâm</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Isa.42.14">Isa 42:14</reference>) to the captivity, which had already lasted a long time - a time of divine silence: the silence of His help so fas as the servants of Jehovah were concerned, but the silence of His wrath as to the great mass of the people.
entries.f894a0141b174f25f36e9e3f4387e0cda00fdf9e: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.12-Isa.57.13">Isa 57:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen13570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13571" type="x-p"/> But this silence would not last for ever. <hi type="italic">“I will proclaim thy righteousness; and thy works, they will not profit thee. When thou criest, let thy heaps of idols save thee: but a wind carries them all away; a breath takes them off; and whoever putteth trust in me will inherit the land, and take possession of my holy mountain.”</hi> According to the context, צדקתך cannot be a synonym of ישׁוּעה f here. It is neither salvation nor the way of salvation that is intended; nor is this even included, as Stier supposes. But the simple reference is to what Israel in its blindness regarded as righteousness; whereas, if it had known itself, it would have seen that it was the most glaring opposite. This lying-righteousness of Israel would be brought to a judicial exposure by Jehovah. ואת־מעשׂיך is not a second accusative to אגּיד, for in that case we should have ומעשׂיך את־צדקתך; but it commences a second sentence, as the accents really indicate. When Jehovah begins thus to speak and act, the impotence of the false gods which His people have made for themselves will soon be exposed; and “as for thy works (i.e., thine idols, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.29">Isa 41:29</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.1.31">Isa 1:31</reference>), they will do thee no good” (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.9-Isa.44.10">Isa 44:9-10</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.23.33">Jer 23:33</reference>; for the question מה־משׂא), here an empatic elevation of the subject, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">Isa 53:8</reference>, ואת־דורו, Ewald, § 277, p. 683). This determines the meaning of קבּוּציך, which Knobel supposes to refer to the large army of the Babylonians, with which the apostates among the exiles had formed an offensive and defensive alliance. But the term is really applied to the heaps (<hi type="italic">qibbūts</hi>, <hi type="italic">collectio</hi>, not an adjective of the form <hi type="italic">limmūd</hi>) of different idols, with which Israel had furnished itself even in its captivity (compare <hi type="italic">qibbâtsâh</hi> in Mic 1:7). It was in vain for them to turn to these pantheons of theirs; a single <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi> would carry them all away, a <hi type="italic">hebhel</hi> would sweep them off, for they themselves were nothing but <hi type="italic">hebhel</hi> and <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.29">Isa 41:29</reference>). The proper punctuation here is יקּח־הבל; the first syllable of יקח, which is attached to a word with a disjunctive accent, has a so-called heavy <hi type="italic">Gaya</hi>, the second a euphonic <hi type="italic">Gaya</hi>, according to rules which are too little discussed in our grammars. When Knobel supports his explanation of קבוציך on the ground that the idols in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.13">Isa 57:13</reference></hi> and the worshippers of Jehovah in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.13">Isa 57:13</reference></hi> do not form a fitting antithesis, the simple reply is, that the contrast lies between the idols, which cannot save, and Jehovah, who not only saves those who trust in Him, but sends them prosperity according to His promises. With the promise, “Whoso trusts in me will inherit the land,” this prophecy reaches the thought with which the previous prophecy (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.7-Isa.51.8">Isa 51:7-8</reference>) closed; and possibly what is here affirmed of קבּוּציך forms an intentional antithesis to the promise there, לנקבּציו עליו אקבּץ עוד: when Jehovah gathers His faithful ones from the dispersion, and gathers others to them (from among the heathen), then will the plunder which the faithless have gathered together be all scattered to the winds. And whilst the latter stand forsaken by their powerless works, the former will be established in the peaceful inheritance of the promised land. The first half of the prophecy closes here. It is full of reproach, and closes with a brief word of promise, which is merely the obverse of the threat. The second half follows an opposite course. Jehovah will redeem His people, provided it has been truly humbled by the sufferings appointed, for He has seen into what errors it has fallen since He has withdrawn His mercy from it. “But the wicked,” etc. The whole closes here with words of threatening, which are the obverse of the promise. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.13">Isa 57:13</reference></hi> forms the transition from the first half to the second.
entries.b463e4521cae92a039b59dbe25638229d321c818: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.14">Isa 57:14</reference> <div eID="gen13571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13572" type="x-p"/> The promise is now followed by a appeal to make ready the way which the redeemed people have to take. <hi type="italic">“And He saith, Heap up, heap up, prepare a way, take away every obstruction from the way of my people.”</hi> This is the very same appeal which occurs once in all three books of these prophecies (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.3-Isa.40.4">Isa 40:3-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.14">Isa 57:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.62.10">Isa 62:10</reference>). The subject of the verb (<hi type="italic">'âmar</hi>) is not Jehovah; but the prophet intentionally leaves it obscure, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6">Isa 40:6</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.26.2">Isa 26:2</reference>). It is a heavenly cry; and the crier is not to be more precisely named.
entries.ae41d65e671ffce7d04b76716867fb8e8072694a: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference> <div eID="gen13572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13573" type="x-p"/> The primary ground for this voice being heard at all is, that the Holy One is also the Merciful One, and not only has a manifestation of glory on high, but also a manifestation of grace below. <hi type="italic">“For thus saith the high and lofty One, the eternally dwelling One, He whose name is Holy One; I dwell on high and in the holy place, and with the contrite one and him that is of a humbled spirit, to revive the spirit of humbled ones, and to revive the heart of contrite ones.”</hi> He inflicts punishment in His wrath; but to those who suffer themselves to be urged thereby to repentance and the desire for salvation, He is most inwardly and most effectually near with His grace. For the heaven of heavens is not too great for Him, and a human heart is not too small for Him to dwell in. And He who dwells upon cherubim, and among the praises of seraphim, does not scorn to dwell among the sighs of a poor human soul. He is called <hi type="italic">râm</hi> (high), as being high and exalted in Himself; נשּׂא (the lofty One), as towering above all besides; and עד שׁכן. This does not mean the dweller in eternity, which is a thought quite outside the biblical range of ideas; but, since עד stands to שׁכן not in an objective, but in an attributive or adverbial relation (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Prov.1.33">Pro 1:33</reference>), and שׁכן, as opposed to being violently wrested from the ordinary sphere of life and work (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.16.9">Psa 16:9</reference>; 102:29), denotes a continuing life, a life having its root in itself, עד שׁכן must mean the eternally (= לעד) dwelling One, i.e., He whose life lasts for ever and is always the same. He is also called <hi type="italic">qâdōsh</hi>, as One who is absolutely pure and good, separated from all the uncleanness and imperfection by which creatures are characterized. This is not to be rendered <hi type="italic">sanctum nomen ejus</hi>, but <hi type="italic">sanctus</hi>; this name is the <hi type="italic">facit</hi> of His revelation of Himself in the history of salvation, which is accomplished in love and wrath, grace and judgment. This God inhabits <hi type="italic">mârōm</hi> <hi type="italic">veqâdōsh</hi>, the height and the Holy Place (accusatives of the object, like <hi type="italic">mârōm</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">Isa 33:5</reference>, and <hi type="italic">merōmı̄m</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Isa 33:16</reference>), both together being equivalent to φῶς ἀπρόσιτον (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:16</reference>), since <hi type="italic">qâdōsh</hi> (neuter, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">Psa 46:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.65.5">Psa 65:5</reference>) answers to φῶς, and <hi type="italic">mârōm</hi> to ἀπρόσιτον. But He also dwells with (את as in <reference osisRef="Lev.16.16">Lev 16:16</reference>) the crushed and lowly of spirit. To these He is most intimately near, and that for a salutary and gracious purpose, namely “to revive ... .” ההיה<hi type="italic">e</hi> and היּה always signify either to keep that which is living alive, or to restore to life that which is dead. The spirit is the seat of pride and humility, the heart the seat of all feeling of joy and sorrow; we have therefore <hi type="italic">spiritum humilium</hi> and <hi type="italic">cor contritorum</hi>. The selfish egotism which repentance breaks has its root in the heart; and the self-consciousness, from whose false elevation repentance brings down, has its seat in the spirit (<hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 199).
entries.50bfe7ea05386e4b462bbefe6b52ace953d83aec: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.16">Isa 57:16</reference> <div eID="gen13573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13574" type="x-p"/> The compassion, by virtue of which God has His abode and His work of grace in the spirit and heart of the penitent, is founded in that free anticipating love which called man and his self-conscious spirit-soul into being at the first. <hi type="italic">“For I do not contend for ever, and I am not angry for ever: for the spirit would pine away before me, and the souls of men which I have created.”</hi> The early translators (lxx, Syr., Jer., possibly also the Targum) give to יעטף the meaning <hi type="italic">egredietur</hi>, which certainly cannot be established. And so also does Stier, so far as the thought is concerned, when he adopts the rendering, “A spirit from me will cover over, and breath of life will I make;” and so Hahn, “When the spirit pines away before me, I create breath in abundance.” But in both cases the writer would at any rate have used the <hi type="italic">perf. consec.</hi> ועשׂיתי, and the last clause of the v. has not the syntactic form of an apodosis. The rendering given above is the only one that is unassailable both grammatically and in fact. כּי introduces the reason for the self-limitation of the divine wrath, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.38-Ps.78.39">Psa 78:38-39</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.103.14">Psa 103:14</reference>): if God should put no restraint upon His wrath, the consequence would be the entire destruction of human life, which was His creative work at first. The verb עטף, from its primary meaning to bend round (<hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference>), has sometimes the transitive meaning to cover, and sometimes the meaning to wrap one’s self round, i.e., to become faint or weak (compare עטוּף, fainted away, <reference osisRef="Lam.2.19">Lam 2:19</reference>; and התעטּף in <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>, which is applied to the spirit, like the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> here). מלּפני is equivalent to “in consequence of the wrath proceeding from me.” נשׁמות (a plural only met with here) signifies, according to the fixed usage of the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa 2:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.5">Isa 42:5</reference>), the souls of men, the origin of which is described as a <hi type="italic">creation</hi> in the attributive clause (with an emphatic אני), just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.38.16">Jer 38:16</reference> (cf., Zec 12:1). Whether the accents are intended to take עשׂיתי אני in this attributive sense or not, cannot be decided from the <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi> attached to ונשׁמות. The prophet, who refers to the flood in other passages also (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Isa 54:9</reference>), had probably in his mind the promise given after the flood, according to which God would not make the existing and inherited moral depravity an occasion for utterly destroying the human race.
entries.ea0bf037cc3e2fa422ea7d74bde985a545e4750b: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.17-Isa.57.18">Isa 57:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen13574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> This general law of His action is most especially the law of His conduct towards Israel, in which such grievous effects of its well-deserved punishment are apparent, and effects so different from those intended, that the compassion of God feels impelled to put an end to the punishment for the good of all that are susceptible of salvation. <hi type="italic">“And because of the iniquity of its selfishness, I was wroth, and smote it; hiding myself, and being angry: then it went on, turning away in the way of its own heart. I have seen its ways, and will heal it; and will lead it, and afford consolations to it, and to its mourning ones.”</hi> The fundamental and chief sin of Israel is here called בּצע, lit., a cut of slice (= gain, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Isa 56:11</reference>); then, like πλεονεξία, which is “idolatry” according to <reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>, or like φιλαργυρία, which is “the root of all evil” according to <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.10">1Ti 6:10</reference>, greedy desire for worldly possession, self-seeking, or worldliness generally. The future ואכּהוּ, standing as it does by the side of the perfect here, indicates that which is also past; and ואקצף stands in the place of a second gerund: <hi type="italic">abscondendo</hi> (viz., <hi type="italic">pânai</hi>, my face, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.8">Isa 54:8</reference>) <hi type="italic">et stomachando</hi>. When Jehovah had thus wrathfully hidden His gracious countenance from Israel, and withdrawn His gracious presence out of the midst of Israel (Hos 5:6, מהם חל), it went away from Him (שׁובב with שׁובב, like עולל with עולל), going its own ways like the world of nations that had been left to themselves. But Jehovah had not seen these wanderings without pity. The futures which follow are promising, not by virtue of any syntactic necessity, but by virtue of an inward necessity. He will heal His wounded (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.4-Isa.1.6">Isa 1:4-6</reference>) and languishing people, and lead in the right way those that are going astray, and afford them consolation as a recompense for their long sufferings (נחוּמים is derived from the <hi type="italic">piel</hi> נחם, and not, as in Hos 11:8, from the <hi type="italic">hiphal</hi> <hi type="italic">hinnâchēm</hi>, in the sense of “feelings of sympathy”), especially (<hi type="italic">Vav epexeget</hi>.; Ges. §155, 1) its mourning ones (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.2-Isa.61.3">Isa 61:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.10">Isa 66:10</reference>), i.e., those who punishment has brought to repentance, and rendered desirous of salvation.
entries.a1a5fb42548600a4225685dd7023536701458d78: <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19-Isa.57.21">Isa 57:19-21</reference> <div eID="gen13575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13576" type="x-p"/> But when the redemption comes, it will divide Israel into two halves, with very different prospects. <hi type="italic">“Creating fruit of the lips; Jehovah saith, 'Peace, peace to those that are far off, and to those that are near; and I heal it.' But the wicked are like the sea that is cast up for it cannot rest, and its waters cast out slime and mud. There is no peace, saith my God, for the wicked.”</hi> The words of God in <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa 57:19</reference> are introduced with an interpolated <hi type="italic">“inquit Jehova”</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa 45:24</reference>, and the ellipsis in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.27">Isa 41:27</reference>); and what Jehovah effects by speaking thus is placed first in a determining participial clause: “Creating fruit (נוב = נוּב, נוב, <hi type="italic">keri</hi> ניב) of the lips,” καρπὸν χείλεων (lxx, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb 13:15</reference>), i.e., not of His own lips, to which בּורא would be inapplicable, but the offering of praise and thanksgiving springing from human lips (for the figure, see <hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 214, trans.; and on the root נב, to press upon forward): “Jehovah saith <hi type="italic">shâlōm</hi>, <hi type="italic">shâlōm</hi>,” i.e., lasting and perfect peace (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa 26:3</reference>), “be the portion of those of my people who are scattered far and near” (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.5-Isa.43.7">Isa 43:5-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.12">Isa 49:12</reference>; compare the application to heathen and Jews in <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Eph 2:17</reference>); “and I heal <hi type="italic">it</hi>” (viz., the nation, which, although scattered, is like one person in the sight of God). But the wicked, who persist in the alienation from God inherited from the fathers, are incapable of the peace which God brings to His people: they are like the sea in its tossed and stormy state (נגרשׁ pausal third pers. as an attributive clause). As this cannot rest, and as its waters cast out slime and mud, so has their natural state become one of perpetual disturbance, leading to the uninterrupted production of unclean and ungodly thoughts, words, and works. Thus, then, there is no peace for them, saith my God. With these words, which have even a more pathetic sound here than in <reference osisRef="Isa.48.22">Isa 48:22</reference>, the prophet seals the second book of his prophecies. The “wicked” referred to are not the heathen outside Israel, but the heathen, i.e., those estranged from God, within Israel itself. <div eID="gen13576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13577" type="x-p"/> The transition form the first to the second half of this closing prophecy is formed by ואמר in Isa 57:14. In the second half, from <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.57.11">Isa 57:11</reference></hi>, we find the accustomed style of our prophet; but in Isaiah 56:9-57:11 <hi type="italic">a</hi> the style is so thoroughly different, that Ewald maintains that the prophet has here inserted in his book a fragment from some earlier writer of the time of Manasseh. But we regard this as very improbable. It is not required by what is stated concerning the prophets and shepherds, for the book of Ezekiel clearly shows that the prophets and shepherds of the captivity were thus debased. Still less does what is stated concerning the early death of the righteous require it; for the fundamental idea of the suffering servant of Jehovah, which is peculiar to the second book, is shadowed forth therein. Nor by what is affirmed as to the idolatrous conduct of the people; for in the very centre (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.4">Isa 57:4</reference>) the great mass of the people are reproached for their contemptuous treatment of the servants of Jehovah. Nor does the language itself force us to any such conjecture, for <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12">Isa 53:1-12</reference> also differs from the style met with elsewhere; and yet (although Ewald regards it as an earlier, borrowed fragment) it must be written by the author of the whole, since its grandest idea finds its fullest expression there. At the same time, we may assume that the prophet described the idolatry of the people under the influences of earlier models. If he had been a prophet of the captives after the time of Isaiah, he would have rested his prophecies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel. For just as Isa 51:18. has the ring of the Lamentations of Jeremiah, so does Isa 57:3. resemble in many respects the earlier reproaches of Jeremiah (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.5.7-Jer.5.9">Jer 5:7-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.29">Jer 5:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.8">Jer 9:8</reference>, with the expression, “Should I rest satisfied with this?”); also <reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jer 2:25</reference> (נואשׁ), <reference osisRef="Jer.2.20">Jer 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.6">Jer 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.13">Jer 3:13</reference> (“upon lofty mountains and under green trees”); also the night scene in Ezek 23.  <chapter eID="Isa.57"/> <div eID="gen13577" type="x-p"/>
