                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> go in peace.</ns0:note> enter into peace <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This just and merciful man shall enter in a state of peace and rest, where he shall be out of the reach of the approaching mise<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries. Or, <ns0:hi>he shall go</ns0:hi> (to wit, <ns0:hi>to his Fathers,</ns0:hi> as it is fully expressed, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15. 15. Or, <ns0:hi>he shall die, going</ns0:hi> being put for <ns0:hi>dying,</ns0:hi> as 1 <ns0:hi>Chr.</ns0:hi> 17. 11. compared with 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 12. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 10. 21. & 14. 20. <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 22. 22. and elsewhere:) in <ns0:hi>peace.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: they <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Just men. Here is a sudden change of the number, which is very frequent in the Prophets.</ns0:note> shall rest in their beds <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">In their Graves, which are not unfitly called their <ns0:hi>Beds,</ns0:hi> or sleep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ping Houses, as their death is commonly called <ns0:hi>sleep</ns0:hi> in Scripture.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>each one</ns0:hi> walking <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Or that <ns0:hi>walketh</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>did walk, i. e.</ns0:hi> live.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> before him.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>in</ns0:hi> his uprightness <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">In a sincere and faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful discharge of his duties to God and Men. Or, <ns0:hi>before him, i. e.</ns0:hi> before God, according to the usual Phrase of Scripture, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 17. 1. 1 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 2. 4. & 8. 25. For God is oft understood where he is not expressed, but only designed by this or the like pronoun, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 15. 13. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 But draw near hither <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To Gods Tribunal, to answer for your selves, and to hear what I have to say against you, and to receive your sentence.</ns0:note>, ye sons of the sorceress <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Not by propagation, but by imitation; such being frequently called a Mansor Womans Sons that learn their Art, or follow their Example: you Sorcerers, either properly or Metaphorically so called; for the Jews were guilty of it both ways.</ns0:note>, the seed of the Adulteress, and the whore <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not the genu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ine Children of <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> as you pretend and boast, but begotten in Fornication upon a common Whore. Which is not to be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood properly but figuratively, because their dispositions and carriages were far more sutable to a bastardly brood, than to <ns0:hi>Abra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ham's</ns0:hi> Seed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Against whom do ye sport your selves <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Consider whom it is that you mock and scoff when you deride Gods Prophets, as they did, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 28. 14, 22. and know that it is not so much Men that you abuse, as God, whose Cause they plead, and in whose name they speak.</ns0:note>? against whom make ye a wide mouth, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> draw out the tongue <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">These are the known and com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon gestures of Mockers, of which see <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 16. 10. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 22. 7. & 35. 21.</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> ye not children of transgression, a seed of falshood <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Either an adulterous brood, as was said before: or, a Generation of Liars, whose practices grosly contradict your prin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ciples and professions, who deal deceitfully and perfidiously both with God and with Men.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Enflaming your selves <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>with gods,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>among the oaks.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> with idols <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>being enflamed,</ns0:hi> &c. lusting after them, and mad upon them, as the Phrase is, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 50. 38. fervent both in making and in worshipping of them, as was observed, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 44. 12, &c. It is a Metaphor borrowed from Whoredom to which Idolatry is oft compared.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">2 Kin. 16. 4.</ns0:note> under eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry green tree <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Wheresoever you see an Idol erected, which was commonly done in Groves, or under great and shady trees, which both defended the Worshippers from the heat of the Sun, and were supposed to strike them with a kind of sacred Horrour and Reverence. See on <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12. 2. 2. <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 16. 4. & 17. 10.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 16. 20. & 20. 26.</ns0:note> slaying the children <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">In way of Sacrifice to their Idols, after the manner of the barbarous Heathens; of which see on <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 18. 21. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 12. 31. 2 <ns0:hi>Kin.</ns0:hi> 21. 6. & 23. 10.</ns0:note> in the valleys <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>besides the brooks,</ns0:hi> which run in valleys: which was most commodious for such bloody work. He seems to allude to the valley of <ns0:hi>Hinnom</ns0:hi> in which these cruelties were practised, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 7. 31. through which also the Brook <ns0:hi>Kidron</ns0:hi> is supposed to have run.</ns0:note> under the clifts of the rocks <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Which they chose either for shade, or for those dark vaults and hollow places, which were either by Nature or Art made in rocks, and which were convenient for, and frequently appointed to ido<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />latrous uses.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:617" />6 Among the smooth stones of the stream <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy por<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Thou hast chosen for thy portion those Idols which were ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther made of those smooth stones which were cast up by Rivers; or which were worshipped upon Altars made of such stones; or which were worshipped by the sides of Brooks or Rivers where such smooth stones commonly lie.</ns0:note>; they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> thy lot <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Thou hast forsaken me and chosen Idols for the great object of thy Worship and Trust.</ns0:note>: even to them hast thou poured a drink-offering, thou hast offered a meat-offer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">For the Devil is Gods Ape, and Idolaters used the same Rites and offerings in the Worship of Idols which God had prescribed in his own, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 15. 4, &c.</ns0:note>. Should I receive comfort in these <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Should I be pleased with such a people and such Actions? Must I not needs be highly provoked, and shew my displeasure by an exemplary punishment of such wicked and foolish Actions? This is an usual Figure, called <ns0:hi>Meiosis,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Litotes,</ns0:hi> when less is said, and more is understood.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek 16. 16, 25.</ns0:note> Upon a lofty and high mountain <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In high places, which were much used for religious Worship, both by Israelites and by Heathens.</ns0:note> hast thou set thy bed <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thine Altar, as appears from the <ns0:hi>Sacrifice</ns0:hi> here following, in which thou didst commit spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual Whoredom with Idols. Compare <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 23, 17, 41.</ns0:note>: even thither wentest thou up to offer sacrifice.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Behind <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 8. 10. & 23. 14.</ns0:note> the doors also and the posts <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which by a Figure called <ns0:hi>Hendiaduo</ns0:hi> may be put for <ns0:hi>the door<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posts,</ns0:hi> as it is expressed, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 11. 20. Behind the posts of the doors of thine House: where the Heathens are said to have placed their tutelary gods to whose protection they committed themselves and their Houses, that so they might have their Eyes and Minds upon them, whensoever they went out or came in. Here also the Israelites might put them in some close corner, that they might keep them secret, it being opprobrious, and oft times dangerous for them to worship Idols.</ns0:note> hast thou set up thy remembrance <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Those Images or Monuments and tokens which thou didst make and set up there as remembrances of those Idol-gods whom they represented, or to whom they be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />longed. He saith, <ns0:hi>thy remembrance,</ns0:hi> in opposition to Gods re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membrances, or to that Writing of Gods Law upon their door<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posts, which God prescribed to keep him and his Law in their re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membrance, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 6. 9. & 11. 20.</ns0:note>: for thou hast discovered <ns0:hi>thy self to another</ns0:hi> than me <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Thou hast uncovered thy nakedness, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> prostituted thy Body (as that Phrase commonly signifies) to others besides me thine Husband. Heb. <ns0:hi>from with me</ns0:hi> (departing from me, or, as it were rising out of my Bed) <ns0:hi>thou hast unco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vered</ns0:hi> or prostituted thy self to others like an impudent and insatiable strumpet.</ns0:note>, and art gone up <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Into the Adulterous Bed, as this very word is used, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 49. 4.</ns0:note>: thou hast enlarged thy bed <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That it might receive many Adulterers together. Thou hast multiplied thine Idols and Altars.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>hewed</ns0:hi> it <ns0:hi>for thy self</ns0:hi> lar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger <ns0:hi>than theirs.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> made <ns0:hi>a covenant</ns0:hi> with them <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Thou hast cove<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nanted to serve them, and to expect help from them. But because the verb here used being thus put by itself, never signifies <ns0:hi>to make a Covenant,</ns0:hi> it seems to be better rendred in the margent of our Bi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, and by others, <ns0:hi>hast hewed</ns0:hi> it (to wit, thy Bed, which is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed both in the next foregoing, and in the next following words:) <ns0:hi>for thy self</ns0:hi> (for thine Idolatrous uses:) larger <ns0:hi>than theirs,</ns0:hi> than their bed, as it follows: or thus, <ns0:hi>didst hew down</ns0:hi> (to wit, trees, which is easily understood both from the Verb, and from the na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture of the thing) <ns0:hi>to</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>for thy self</ns0:hi> (to make Images or other things relating to thy false Gods) <ns0:hi>more than they,</ns0:hi> more than the Heathens, of whom thou hast learned these practices, as God complains, 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 21. 9. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 16. 46, 47, 52.</ns0:note>; <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ezek. 16. 26, 28. & 23. 12, &c.</ns0:note> thou lovedst their bed <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> thou pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />videst room.</ns0:note> where thou sawest it <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">No sooner didst thou see their Idols but thou wast enamoured with them, and didst fall down and worship them, like an unchaste and lewd Woman, who upon all occasions, and at the very first view of any man, is infla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med with Lust towards them. Heb. <ns0:hi>thou lovedst their Bed (i. e.</ns0:hi> their filthy conversation) in <ns0:hi>the place</ns0:hi> (for so this Hebrew word frequently signifies, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 23. 12. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 22. 18. and elsewhere,) where <ns0:hi>thou sawest</ns0:hi> it. Or, thus, <ns0:hi>thou lovedst their bed, thou didst provide</ns0:hi> (as this word signifies, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 18. 21. and so doth a word of the very same signification, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 22. 8.) <ns0:hi>a place</ns0:hi> for it, to receive their Bed, to set up their Idols in thine own house.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> thou re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spectedst the King.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 30. 6. Ezek. 16. 33. & 23. 16.</ns0:note> thou wentest <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either by thy self, or, by thy messengers, as it follows. Or, <ns0:hi>thou didst look,</ns0:hi> to wit, earnestly, with expectation and vehement affection.</ns0:note> to the king <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either to <ns0:hi>Moloch,</ns0:hi> which was as it were the King or chief of their Idols, and which signifies a King. Or, to the great King of <ns0:hi>Assyria,</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>the King</ns0:hi> by way of eminency, to whom the Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raelites in the days of <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> were very prone to seek, and trust, and send presents. Although the word, <ns0:hi>King,</ns0:hi> may be here taken collectively for the Kings of <ns0:hi>Assyria</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Egypt,</ns0:hi> or any other King, from whom they desired or expected help in their straits. And so the Prophet passeth here from their Idolatry to another sin, even to their carnal confidence in Heathen Princes, for which they are oft severely reproved; although these two sins were commonly joined together, and they easily received Idolatry from those Kings whose help they desired.</ns0:note> with oint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">With pretious Ointments, and particularly with balm, which was of great price, and was a commodity pecu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liar to those parts, and was sometimes sent as a present. See <ns0:hi>Gen<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> 43. 11. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 8. 22. & 46. 11.</ns0:note>, and didst encrease thy perfumes <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Didst send great quantities there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />of to them to procure their aid.</ns0:note>, and didst send thy messengers far off <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Into <ns0:hi>Assyria,</ns0:hi> which was far from <ns0:hi>Iudaea.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and didst debase <ns0:hi>thy self even</ns0:hi> unto hell <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Thou wast willing to submit to the basest terms to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cure their aid.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Thou hast not eased or relieved, but only tired thy self with all thy tedious journeys, and laborious endeavours.</ns0:note>; <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> saidst thou not, There is no hope <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">And yet thou wast so stupid under all thy discouragements and disappointments, that thou didst not perceive that thy labour was lost, and that thy case was not mended but made worse and desperate by these pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctices.</ns0:note>; thou hast found the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> living<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> life of thine hand <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Thou hast found (i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou falsly imaginest that thou hast found, or shalt assuredly find by these courses) <ns0:hi>the life (i. e.</ns0:hi> the strength or vigor) <ns0:hi>of thine hand,</ns0:hi> that thine hand is strengthened by these pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctices: or, <ns0:hi>life</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>thine hand, i. e.</ns0:hi> by these endeavours and appli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cations of thy self to others for help. Or, thou hast sometimes found success in these ways.</ns0:note>, therefore thou wast not grieved <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Therefore thou didst not repent of thy sin and folly herein, but didst persist and applaud thy self in such courses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And of whom hast thou been afraid or feared <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">And what or who are they, the fear of whom drives thee to these wicked and desperate courses? Are they not men, weak and mortal Creatures, such as wholly depend upon me, and can do no<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing to thee either against me or without me?</ns0:note>, that thou hast lied <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That thou hast dealt thus disloyally and perfidiously with me, and sought for such foreign assistances, contrary to my command, and thy solemn Co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venant.</ns0:note>, and hast not remembred me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Hast thou forgotten all those great things which I have done for thee, and all those Promises which I have made to thee, and constantly performed, when thou hast not grosly violated the conditions upon which they were made.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> nor laid <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> to thy heart <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Or thus, <ns0:hi>nor set</ns0:hi> me <ns0:hi>up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on thine heart,</ns0:hi> as these very words are rendred <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 8. 6. And so this is a repetition of what is said in the foregoing clause in other words. The sense is, Thou hast not seriously and affectionately considered what I am, how all-sufficient, and faithful, and gracious, for then thou wouldest not have distrusted or disobeyed me.</ns0:note>? have not I held my peace even of old <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Have not I forborn to reprove and punish thee for this and for thy other sins, from time to time, ever since thou wast my People, that by this goodness I might oblige thee to love me, and to cleave unto me?</ns0:note>, and thou fearest me not <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>therefore thou dost not fear</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>regard me.</ns0:hi> Thus thou abusest mine indulgence and long-suffering, taking occasion from thence to despise me.</ns0:note>!</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 I will declare <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I will no longer be silent and patient towards thee.</ns0:note> thy righteousness and thy works <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which may be put for <ns0:hi>the righteousness of thy works</ns0:hi> by that known figure, of which see the first note on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 8. whereby he means their wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, which he calleth their <ns0:hi>righteousness</ns0:hi> either Ironically, or be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause it was covered with a pretence of Righteousness, and they al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />leadged that this was a just and lawful thing when they were di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stressed to seek for help from their Neighbours or Allies. The sense is, I will discover whether thy works be righteous, as thou pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tendest they are: my punishments shall manifest the wickedness of thy Actions.</ns0:note>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> and.</ns0:note> for they shall not profit thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">These Actions shall do thee no good but much hurt.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 When thou criest <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To wit, unto me for deliverance</ns0:note>, let thy companies deliver thee <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Expect it not from me whom thou hast forsaken and despised, but from those foreign troops to whom thou hast sought and trusted for succour.</ns0:note>: but the wind shall carry them all away <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">But they shall be so far from saving thee that they shall not be able to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />liver themselves, but shall be carried away suddenly and violently by the blast of mine anger.</ns0:note>; vani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A vapour or puff of Breath which quickly vanisheth away. It is the same thing in effect with the <ns0:hi>wind.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> shall take <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>take</ns0:hi> them <ns0:hi>away,</ns0:hi> as this verb signified, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 11. 13. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>; but he that putteth his trust in me, shall possess the land, and shall inherit my holy mountain <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Shall enjoy my favour and presence in my Temple.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And shall say <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>And he shall say:</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> one <ns0:hi>shall say.</ns0:hi> God will raise up a man who shall say these words, and that with authority and effica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy, so as the thing shall be done.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 40. 3. & 62. 10.</ns0:note> Cast ye up, cast ye up <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Make causeways, where it is needful, for their safe and easie passage.</ns0:note>, pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare the way, take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Remove all things which may hinder them in their return.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:618" />15 For thus saith the high and lofty One that inha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />biteth eternity, whose name <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Holy <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Who is omnipotent, everlasting and unchangeable, holy in all his words and ways, and therefore both can and will deliver his People, as he hath promised to do.</ns0:note>, I dwell in the high and holy <ns0:hi>place;</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ps. 34. 18. & 51. 17. & 138. 6. Ch. 66. 2.</ns0:note> with him also <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> of a con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trite and humble spirit <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">With such also whose Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rits are broken and humbled by Afflictions, and by a sense of their sins for which they were afflicted; which doubtless was the case of many of the Jews in the Babylonish Captivity: whom therefore he here implies that God would pity and deliver out of their Di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stresses.</ns0:note>, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones.</ns0:p>
